implementation_notes: JavaScript's collection pipeline is the array method chain: Array.prototype.map (transform), filter (drop), flatMap (expand), reduce/reduceRight (the documented terminal that combines elements into one value), plus some/every/find for short-circuiting. All of them are eager and return a new array, which replaces index loops with accumulator variables. Use for...of instead when a stage would only be a forEach with side effects, and a Set for deduplication instead of scanning with indexOf.
code_sketch:
const emails = people
  .filter(p => p.active)
  .map(p => p.email)
  .filter(e => e != null)
  .sort()
  .slice(0, 10);                  // eager: one new array per stage

const total = orders.reduce((sum, o) => sum + o.amount, 0);
pitfalls: sort mutates the receiver and compares as strings by default ([10, 9].sort() is [10, 9]): pass a comparator and copy first ([...xs].sort(cmp)) when the source must stay unchanged.
Every stage allocates a new array, and reduce without an initial value throws on an empty array (or silently returns the first element), so the empty case must be decided explicitly.
Callbacks receive extra arguments (index, array), which breaks idioms like ['1','2'].map(parseInt); wrap the function or pass an explicit lambda.

variants.name: Iterator helper methods (lazy, over any iterator)
variants.implementation_notes: Iterator helpers put the same methods on the Iterator prototype, so anything iterable - generators, Map/Set iterators, results of Iterator.from - can be chained: map, filter, flatMap, take, drop return a chainable iterator helper and reduce/some/find terminate it. MDN states the advantage over array methods directly: iterator helpers 'are lazy, meaning that they only produce the next value when requested', which avoids unnecessary computation and works with infinite iterators. Use it when the source is lazy (a line reader, a large Map, an unbounded generator) and the array form would materialise everything; the helpers shipped in V8 12.2 and became Baseline in March 2025.
pitfalls: The helpers are lazy: without a consuming method (toArray, reduce, for...of) nothing runs, and an un-terminated pipeline over an infinite source never ends.
Availability is runtime-dependent (Baseline 2025, V8 12.2; older Node/browsers need a polyfill), and a missing polyfill fails at call time rather than compile time.
The helpers consume the underlying iterator: the source cannot be re-iterated afterwards, unlike an array.

variants.name: Generator-function pipeline stages
variants.idiom_name: function* stages composed with for...of / yield*
variants.implementation_notes: A generator function is a hand-written lazy stage: it accepts an iterable, yields transformed elements, and yield* delegates to another generator, so stages compose without arrays while for...of, spread and destructuring act as terminals (breaking out of the loop calls generator.return(), which lets try/finally clean up). This is the way to build pull-based pipelines in JavaScript without helper methods, and it is still the right tool for custom stateful stages; it replaces map/filter chains where the stage does not exist as an array method, at the cost of writing the iteration by hand.
pitfalls: A generator abandoned mid-iteration only runs its cleanup if it is closed (break/return in for...of does this; holding the generator object and dropping it does not), so resources belong in try/finally.
A generator is single-use: a second for...of over the same object continues from where it stopped (or ends immediately), so pipelines must be rebuild from the source each time.
